line.tailor_greet: Come in, come in. Look around; nothing here bites.

now.boy_led: The boy went behind the chai stall.

tale.dhruva.1.1: Dhruva was five. He climbed onto his father’s lap, and his stepmother lifted him off. “Not you,” she said. “That seat is for my son.”
tale.dhruva.1.2: He ran to his mother, burning. “Then I will find a seat higher than my father’s,” he said. “Higher than anyone’s.” She did not laugh.
tale.dhruva.1.3: “Only one person gives seats like that,” she said, “and people go to the forest to find him.” So the boy walked into the forest, alone.
tale.dhruva.1.4: On the road a wandering sage met him and taught him a few words to say. The boy stood on one foot and said them, and did not stop.
tale.dhruva.1.5: Months went by. He forgot to eat. The forest went quiet around him. And the one he was calling came, and stood in front of him.
tale.dhruva.1.6: Dhruva had come to ask for a throne. Standing there, he forgot to. “I went looking for broken glass,” he said afterwards, “and was given a jewel.”
tale.dhruva.title: Dhruva, the boy who wanted a higher seat
tale.prahlada.1.1: Prahlada was five years old. His father was king of the whole world and wanted to be called God. The whole court called him so.
tale.prahlada.1.2: The king sent the boy to school to learn to rule. The teachers taught him law, and gold, and how to make enemies afraid.
tale.prahlada.1.3: When the teachers left the room, the boy told the other children what he knew: that someone loves us, and the rest is not worth the chase.
tale.prahlada.1.4: The teachers were frightened and took him to his father. “What have you learned?” asked the king. The boy told him, plainly. The king threw him from a cliff.
tale.prahlada.1.5: Elephants, poison, fire, snakes. Nothing touched him. He went on saying the same thing, gently, as if his father could still hear it.
tale.prahlada.1.6: At last the king roared, “Where is this god of yours? In this pillar?” “In the pillar,” said the boy. “And in you.” And the pillar split.
tale.prahlada.title: Prahlada, the boy in the king’s school
tale.puranjana.1.1: There was once a king called Puranjana. He had a friend from before he could remember, who went everywhere with him and asked for nothing.
tale.puranjana.1.2: One day the king wanted a place of his own. He walked off without a word, to look for a city that would suit him.
tale.puranjana.1.3: He searched the whole world and nothing pleased him. Then, below the mountains, he found it: a city with nine gates, gardens, lakes and birds.
tale.puranjana.1.4: In the garden a woman was walking with ten servants, and a serpent with five heads went before her. She asked him who he was.
tale.puranjana.1.5: He could not say. He had forgotten where he came from. “Then stay,” she said. “Rule the city with me.” And he did.
tale.puranjana.1.6: The friend did not follow him in. But he did not go away, either. He stood at the gate, where no one looked.
tale.puranjana.2.1: Puranjana ruled through seven gates above and two below. Through two he went out to look, through two to listen, through one to taste.
tale.puranjana.2.2: Whatever the queen wanted, he wanted. When she was glad, he was glad. When she turned her face away, he begged until she turned back.
tale.puranjana.2.3: He rode out hunting and killed more than he needed. He came home proud of it, and that night she would not look at him.
tale.puranjana.2.4: A hundred years went by in the city. He did not count them. The friend at the gate counted every one.
tale.puranjana.2.5: Then an army came to the walls: three hundred and sixty soldiers, and their wives, day after night after day. Nobody saw them arrive.
tale.puranjana.2.6: The serpent at the gate grew tired. The king grew slow and grey. Time’s daughter walked in, and no one could turn her out.
tale.puranjana.3.1: At the end the city fell. Fear’s soldiers dragged Puranjana out through the gate, and the queen and the children were left behind.
tale.puranjana.3.2: His last thought was of her. Because of that thought he was born again as a woman, a princess, and he remembered nothing.
tale.puranjana.3.3: She married a good king and raised his children. When he died she sat by the fire where they burned him, and wept, and would not go home.
tale.puranjana.3.4: A stranger came and sat down beside her. “Who are you?” he asked. “Who are you weeping for? Do you not know me?”
tale.puranjana.3.5: “You and I were two swans on the same lake,” he said. “You went looking for a city of your own. I came after. I have been here all along.”
tale.puranjana.3.6: “You were never the king, nor the queen, nor the woman by the fire. You were my friend. Look at me.” She looked, and remembered.
tale.puranjana.3.7: That is the tale. The city with nine gates is this one, here. Count them if you like. And the friend is still at the gate.
tale.puranjana.title: Puranjana, the king who forgot himself
